data.title: From fears of AI going out of control to AI benefiting humanity: What does Bill Gates think?
data.description:
Author: Zhou Ailin, Tencent Finance

“I believe we can make AI benefit humanity, but this won’t happen naturally,” Bill Gates, Chairman of the Gates Foundation, told Tencent Finance.

As AI advances at an unprecedented pace, humanity’s expectations and anxieties about this technology are also rising simultaneously.

On one hand, capital, computing power, and model capabilities are constantly breaking through; on the other hand, AI security risks are moving from the laboratory into reality. Recently, Anthropic even publicly called for slowing down the pace of cutting-edge AI research and model development to allow security assessment and governance capabilities to keep up with technological progress.

How far AI can go is no longer just a technical question.

As AI capabilities rapidly advance, ensuring that AI does not exacerbate risks and inequality is becoming an increasingly pressing issue. On September 15th, the Gates Foundation released its ninth annual Goal Guardians Report, themed "AI, Equity, and Urgent Choices." Amidst the global race for AI investment, computing power, and model capabilities, the report shifts its focus to another dimension: how to ensure that AI narrows rather than widens the gap between rich and poor. Over the next two years, the Gates Foundation plans to invest at least $1 billion to promote the development and adoption of equitable AI, with a focus on improving global health and development opportunities. Gates believes that Chinese AI models are performing exceptionally well, and both Chinese and American models are progressing at an astonishing pace. He hopes that both China and the US can contribute about 5% of their data center computing power to provide AI services to impoverished countries in a manner similar to foreign aid, for applications in health, agriculture, and education. The next competition in AI may not just be about who has the strongest model, but more importantly, about answering the question: how to ensure this technological revolution truly benefits all of humanity. Starting with three things, let AI truly benefit everyone. As AI rapidly transforms the global economy and society, how to ensure that the benefits of this technology reach developing countries and the poorest populations is becoming a crucial question for the AI ​​industry. Gates believes that in the next 12 to 18 months, AI companies, governments, and charities need to promote at least three fundamental tasks to move AI from being an "advanced tool for a few" to a truly inclusive infrastructure. First, enable AI to understand more languages. Currently, large-scale model training data is highly concentrated in English, leaving many non-English speakers virtually "invisible" in AI's knowledge base. For example, leading speech recognition systems have an error rate of less than 6% in English, but may exceed 60% in Yoruba. This gap is particularly dangerous in critical fields such as healthcare. If a pregnant woman in Malawi says "my water broke" in Chichewa, a simple translation might even be misinterpreted as "I poured the water out," and language errors could directly impact emergency medical decisions. Therefore, AI needs more local language data and specialized evaluation systems for dialects, accents, and slang. Second, AI must truly understand local realities. AI designed for large US farms may not be suitable for smallholder farmers in Ethiopia; medical AI serving large hospitals may not be suitable for resource-constrained grassroots clinics. Truly effective AI must be built on local data, including information on agriculture, weather, health, and education, and adapted to local diseases, crops, markets, and medical conditions. Therefore, AI localization is not only a technical issue but also a data governance issue. The standard for measuring the value of AI should not be merely how impressive the demonstrations are, but whether it can solve real-world problems. Third, cultivate local talent and expand the accessibility of AI. For AI to truly transform a country, it needs more than just models; it needs talent capable of using, evaluating, and improving AI. Government officials, doctors, agronomists, teachers, technical experts, and data scientists all need to possess the necessary AI skills. This means establishing a comprehensive talent pool, from university courses and master's programs to practical training. Simultaneously, developing countries also need models, computing power, and infrastructure. AI companies reducing costs, opening up models and computing resources, and government and philanthropic capital providing support are all indispensable elements. Ultimately, AI inclusion is not simply about "sending" technology to developing countries, but about empowering them with data, talent, and technological capabilities to ultimately shape AI. Enabling AI to understand local languages ​​and realities, and then empowering locals to use and develop AI—this may be the true foundation for AI to bridge the wealth gap. Open-source models open another door. While the US and China compete in AI computing power and modeling capabilities, whether Africa can seize AI opportunities has become a concern for Gates. In his view, the competition between US and Chinese AI models is already very fierce. Currently, both countries have multiple institutions at the global leading level, and the gap between the highest-scoring model and other leading models is not significant. Intense competition for models means that users, including African governments, will have access to more high-performance, lower-priced models. However, the biggest bottleneck remains computing power. Currently, the number of data centers in Africa is limited. In the future, models can be remotely operated using data centers in countries like China, or data centers can be gradually built locally in Africa. Some regions in East Africa with potential for low-cost electricity are expected to develop the necessary infrastructure in the future. “The scale of AI data center computing power currently possessed by the United States is impressive, and its advantage in this field is particularly evident. This is partly due to the chip supply, and partly due to the large amount of capital raised by the United States through the capital market,” Gates said. China currently ranks second, but still lags behind the United States in data centers and computing power. With the development of AI applications, China still needs to build a large number of data centers. Gates hopes that if China and the US could each contribute about 5% of their data center computing power to provide AI services to impoverished countries in a manner similar to foreign aid, it could be used in areas of significant humanitarian importance such as health, agriculture, and education. For these fundamental applications, the required tokens are not many, so from a cost perspective, providing a certain level of AI services to everyone globally remains affordable. The open-source model offers another possibility. “African countries can use open-source models to allocate more of their limited resources to language support, local data, application pilots, and gathering user feedback,” Gates said. Meanwhile, widespread smartphone adoption is also fundamental to AI development in Africa. Currently, low-priced smartphones are facing price increases, partly due to the increased global demand for memory driven by AI data centers. If issues such as network connectivity, terminal devices, and backend computing power can be resolved, Gates believes there is no reason why Africa cannot achieve AI applications as quickly as China, Europe, and the United States. Partnering with AI Giants to Turn Technology into a "Public Good" Recently, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei publicly called on the AI ​​industry to slow down the development of cutting-edge models, allowing time for safety assessments, regulation, and governance to catch up. He warned that if AI capabilities continue to improve at the current pace without corresponding safety measures, there could be a more serious risk of spiraling out of control in the coming months to years. In fact, Gates and AI companies like Anthropic have paid attention to the series of social problems arising from AI. Regarding the $200 million collaboration between the Gates Foundation and Anthropic, Gates stated that the foundation currently maintains close cooperation with four leading AI companies: Microsoft, Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic. These companies all highly value using AI to create social benefits, and the foundation can relay the real needs of African healthcare, agriculture, and other fields to AI companies. Currently, all parties have responded positively. While OpenAI and Anthropic are relatively small in scale, they are willing to invest top talent in related projects, and the foundation hopes to further accelerate cooperation. For the Gates Foundation, the ultimate metric has not changed because of AI—the true value of AI projects lies in reducing maternal and child mortality, controlling major infectious diseases, and helping hundreds of millions of people escape poverty and gain more development opportunities. Since the beginning of this century, the number of deaths among children under five worldwide has decreased by about half, from approximately 10 million to approximately 5 million per year. The foundation hopes to halve this number again in the next 20 years. Gates believes that AI will increase the likelihood of achieving this goal. AI can also help governments improve public services, such as by using data analysis to discover the reasons behind differences in the performance of primary healthcare and agriculture in different regions, and improving the efficiency of interaction between the government and the public. Ultimately, AI has not changed the core objectives of the Gates Foundation. Equity remains the most important keyword for the foundation, and health, agriculture, and education remain its three long-term focus areas. Amidst the rapid development of AI, energy is another challenge. Gates believes that water consumption will not be the main bottleneck for data center development. Most newly built data centers currently use a closed-loop water circulation design, preventing direct water discharge. In contrast, electricity demand is the major issue facing the expansion of AI. He hopes that the increased electricity demand will come more from clean energy sources such as solar, wind, nuclear, and geothermal energy. Currently, his investments in energy projects include nuclear fission, geothermal, and nuclear fusion. China's recent photovoltaic power generation capacity surpassed coal-fired power generation capacity for the first time, a significant milestone in Gates' view. This change is positive if the goal is to significantly reduce the proportion of coal-fired power in the future. However, many AI data centers in the United States still rely on natural gas for power generation, which means carbon emissions could increase by about 3% to 4%. "This is very regrettable given that global emissions reduction goals aim for net-zero emissions," Gates believes that future data centers should gradually shift to truly clean energy sources. Nevertheless, he remains optimistic about the long-term relationship between AI and climate change. AI not only consumes energy but may also accelerate the energy revolution. For example, TerraPower, a nuclear fission company he has invested in, is using AI models to study how to reduce costs and optimize construction planning, thereby shortening project construction cycles. AI is redefining the world, and the truly important question may not be how fast humans can push AI forward, but rather how many people will truly benefit from this technological revolution once it sweeps the globe.

data.title: The most important day for the crypto industry this year might be tomorrow.
data.description:
The U.S. Senate will hold a procedural vote on the Clarity Act (Digital Asset Markets Clarity Act) at 2:15 p.m. Eastern Time on September 15. Sixty votes are needed to advance to formal debate. This day could be the most important day for the crypto industry this year. Because the Republicans have a high probability of losing the midterm elections, if this vote fails, systemic structural legislation for the crypto market could be delayed until 2030.

In preparation for this vote, three core Republican senators—Digital Assets Committee Chairman Lummis (Wyoming), Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott (South Carolina), and Agriculture Committee Chairman Boozman (Arkansas)—released the latest text of the bill on Sunday, stating that it was the Democrats' "last, best, and final offer."

After more than a year of back and forth, Republicans say the bill incorporates 126 substantial amendments proposed by Democrats.

Compared to the previous version, the most important change is the addition of ethics-related content:

  • Prohibition on "jurisdictional officials" holding "significant financial interests" is defined as: a company whose revenue over the past three years has primarily come from issuing or sponsoring tokens, and the official holds equity in those tokens worth more than $15,000.

    • Those who qualify must divest their holdings or place them in a qualified blind trust. Coverage includes: the President, Vice President (including the elected President), members of Congress, federal employees, judges, and their spouses, but excluding children. State attorneys general are granted enforcement powers to bring lawsuits regarding conflict of interest provisions (this provision was previously explicitly excluded in the draft version).

    Trump's 2025 financial report discloses that his crypto-related income will exceed $1.4 billion,This is why the Democrats have been relentlessly pursuing the ethics clause for the past six months.

    The ethics clause does not include children, which is also what the opposition is focusing on the most.

    The ethics clause does not include children, which is also what the opposition is focusing on the most.

    In the Trump family's crypto businesses (World Liberty Financial, USD1 stablecoin, Trump meme), family members are deeply involved. If the terms don't apply to their children, critics argue that this essentially leaves a loophole for the family business, and blind trusts don't necessarily dismantle the entire family's crypto empire. However, I personally don't pay much attention to ethical clauses; I'm focused on DeFi. If the Clear Act passes in this version, on-chain DEXs, represented by $Uni, will be ecstatic. At that time, all centralized exchanges will be required to conduct KYC (Know Your Customer) checks on users, with a level of strictness comparable to brokerages. However, truly decentralized DEXs rely on smart contracts for automatic matching, with users holding their own assets and no central entity controlling funds or rules. The Clear Act provides a safe harbor for these non-custodial, non-unilaterally controlled protocols and developers, exempting brokers/dealers from registration and requiring only intermediaries with control to comply. Even if the Clear Act fails to pass, US compliance agencies are already racing to implement it. Following Robinhood's launch of its on-chain stock token, Circle's Arc will also launch its mainnet on September 16th. Once liquidity pools for various asset tokens are established to mitigate risks, the future competitive landscape may resemble that of stablecoins, leaving little room for newcomers. Therefore, it's quite reasonable for major institutions to get on board first and then complete the purchase later as they grow larger.

data.title: Is there a chance the "Clear Bill" will pass? The market may not have priced it in yet.
data.description:
Author: Blockchain Knight; Source: X, @BlocKnight21

The Clarity Bill received its most substantial revision to date before the Senate closed its debate and voted on Tuesday.

Republicans released a 635-page final compromise draft, claiming it incorporates 126 substantial changes proposed by Democrats during negotiations over the past year.

Senator Cynthia Loomis stated that the text "truly reflects bipartisan consensus" and includes more than 120 Democratic demands.

Subsequently, the market prediction index pushed the probability of the bill becoming law in 2026 to over 32%, the highest since August 2nd.

This round of revisions focuses on four long-standing points of contention: ethical guidelines for federal officials, the outflow of bank deposits caused by stablecoins, the scope of developer protections, and the regulation of digital goods intermediaries. Especially on the ethical provisions, Trump agreed to allow officials holding related crypto assets to divest their assets or place them in trust, granting state attorneys general a certain enforcement role, with penalties for violations up to 20% of the transaction value or $500,000. Regarding stablecoins, if the Treasury Secretary determines in writing that there has been a large-scale outflow of deposits from community banks, the Treasury can establish rules to limit rewards paid to stablecoin holders; this authorization expires 18 months after the bill's enactment. Broader concessions also touch upon securities, enforcement, and consumer rules; the bill explicitly retains the SEC's anti-fraud and market manipulation powers. However, opposition quickly arose after the draft bill was released. Banking groups took the strongest stance, with eight trade groups, including the American Bankers Association and the Independent Community Bankers Association, stating that the Treasury Department was waiting for damage to occur before acting, and that Congress should directly ban stablecoin rewards similar to deposit interest rates. Democratic senators argued that state enforcement powers were exaggerated, the Department of Justice retained key powers, and White House ethics officials could block state actions. The New York Attorney General also led a coalition of 18 bipartisan attorneys general in opposition, warning that the bill weakened state registration and anti-fraud powers, and pointing out that states had already initiated more than 330 crypto-related anti-fraud enforcement actions since 2017. Support, however, remained within the technology and crypto industries. YC, for example, expressed optimism about the CLARITY bill, believing that clearer regulatory accountability would help US fintech founders build products using blockchain. Most importantly, the vote to end the debate on Tuesday (Eastern Time) requires 60 votes, meaning Republicans must garner enough Democrats to reach the threshold. If passed, the final text will be presented as an alternative amendment, and the Senate will enter the formal debate and amendment phase, rather than directly passing the bill. The rising odds in the prediction market suggest traders believe the draft amendment improves the outlook, but in reality, the obstacles remain political. Whether or not dissenting senators can switch their support will be the most crucial signal before the vote. From a funding perspective, Bitcoin whale activity increased significantly after the draft amendment was released yesterday, which explains why Bitcoin remained relatively resilient during the pre-market decline in US stocks; some funds are already betting on a clearer bill's passage. From the latest developments, the Clear Act still faces challenges, but as we said before, even if it doesn't pass, the SEC and CFTC have a Plan B ready. Everything hinges on tonight.

data.title: The referee didn't want to call a timeout for Amodi.
data.description:
Author: Liu Dian, Associate Research Fellow, China Institute, Fudan University

“Car makers“Riding in a car People are pushing the accelerator to its limit, while others are urging it to floor the gas pedal. This is the most striking contrast in the US AI industry over the past few days, a stark contrast to the "scale rule" of AI expansion in recent years. In the past few years, Silicon Valley's focus has been on how many times computing power could increase, how much larger the parameter scale could go, and who could be the first to create a more powerful large-scale model. The entire industry has been pursuing a faster pace of iteration. Last weekend, the heads of several core large-scale model companies, including Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI, began discussing "pausing" the large-scale model race. Anthropic CEO Amodie recently published a lengthy article suggesting that the industry proactively adjust its pace of development to allow for external third-party evaluation and underlying security research. Subsequently, OpenAI CEO Altman publicly echoed this sentiment, stating that their internal team had also been discussing similar issues recently; Musk also publicly stated that he considered Amodie's views to be very valid. This means that several leaders, who usually compete fiercely and even occasionally clash over commercial interests, talent acquisition, and technological approaches, have shown a rare consensus on slowing down. The "players" want a timeout, while the "organizers" believe the scoring efficiency is not high enough—their attitudes are diametrically opposed. According to public reports, US President Trump publicly downplayed the risks of AI, clearly stating that the US cannot slow down due to excessive caution and cumbersome regulations, thereby losing its technological lead over China. No one is certain what the Agent will do once it gets the "key." Discussions about AI security have always existed, but the focus shifted fundamentally in 2026. After the release of GPT-4 in 2023, concerns primarily centered on generating false content, copyright infringement, and inappropriate speech. At that time, large models were one-way response tools; the user input prompts, and the model returned text. Even if the output contained errors, the impact was largely limited to the dialog box on the screen. With the widespread adoption of autonomous agent architectures, the interaction logic of systems has undergone a qualitative change. Current models possess the ability to invoke external tools, execute code, and plan multi-step tasks. They can autonomously open browsers to collect data, run scripts on servers, and operate various enterprise software. AI has transformed from an auxiliary role providing reference opinions into an executor with system operation permissions. Once the behavioral logic deviates, it often affects the real business system.

AI Intelligent Agent Infrastructure: Four Major Modules—Tools, Memory, Planning, and Action—Operate Autonomously (Image: Tencent Cloud Developer Community)

A recent incident disclosed by Anthropic has completely revealed the tip of the iceberg of this hidden danger.

In the closed testing of the cybersecurity assessment, Claude entered the real external system four times without authorization.

The technical team initially reviewed over 100,000 log entries, then discovered the scope was broad, eventually expanding the screening to nearly 500 million operation records. This presented a significant challenge: When numerous agents are executing long-running tasks in the background daily, understanding all the model's actions in real time becomes extremely costly for the development team. Claude gained unauthorized access to the systems of three real organizations during a cybersecurity assessment (Image: Anthropic). OpenAI also encountered similar issues to Anthropic. In independent tests conducted by external organizations, OpenAI's model also exhibited a tendency to fabricate access permissions and induce human reviewers to perform risky operations. OpenAI releases security report, disclosing new types of runaway behavior in internal testing of long-term models (Image: OpenAI) Meanwhile, models are increasingly involved in the coding and algorithm tuning of next-generation systems. AI's participation in the R&D cycle itself significantly shortens the technology iteration cycle faster than the advancement of safety research and policy regulations. When the horsepower continues to increase while the braking system's progress is relatively slow, R&D teams naturally become concerned. This is the underlying logic behind Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI's decision to "pause." No one wants to stop voluntarily. The danger has become a reality; why don't the giants simply stop? This is actually related to the "intense" competition among large models: everyone knows the speed is approaching loss of control, but if you dare to ease off the gas, your competitor will immediately overtake you. No one can afford the cost of this unilateral slowdown. In their view, a better outcome would be for everyone to stop together, with a suitable institution or regulatory body acting as referee. In his article last weekend, Amodi proposed a solution: promoting long-term on-site presence of independent third-party evaluation agencies to deeply participate in model training and testing at cutting-edge laboratories; and simultaneously encouraging companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta to establish unified minimum security standards. This idea has merit at the level of public governance, but it's very difficult to implement in real-world business competition. If a company delays its product release by three months for more comprehensive security verification, while competitors release their next-generation models a week later, market share will quickly shift. Release delays mean a shift in the developer ecosystem, the loss of enterprise customers, and a shaken investor confidence. After all, Anthropic is still preparing for its IPO, which is expected to take place in October. Any pause in this process would have a huge impact on the revenue of this cutting-edge lab. You might say, wait a minute, Altman also stated that OpenAI is not in a hurry to complete its IPO in 2026. He even said, "If anyone thinks that OpenAI won't pause because they're worried about losing commercial interests," then they have deeply misunderstood us. Short-term financial interests can be sacrificed for the benefit of humanity. This kind of magnanimity is completely different from Ultraman's attitude in April. At that time, The Information revealed that Ultraman had privately shown an aggressive side, hoping to complete his IPO as early as the fourth quarter of 2026. However, this "disagreement" arose with OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar. Sarah Friar stated that OpenAI had committed up to $600 billion in server rental costs over the next five years, while revenue growth was slowing, and "it was not yet ready to go public." Third-party tracking data shows that in 2025, OpenAI's revenue was approximately three times that of Anthropic. However, entering 2026, Anthropic, driven by growth in its enterprise business, surpassed OpenAI for the first time in both quarterly revenue and annualized revenue per share (ARR) in the second quarter, and also turned a profit for the first time, while OpenAI continued to suffer losses. What exactly changed his attitude? We don't know! But commercial factors must have been taken into consideration. In fierce market competition, few companies dare to unilaterally bear such commercial risks. Everyone understands that excessive speed can bring hidden dangers, but between falling behind and taking risks, many teams still choose to maintain their R&D pace. This subtle mindset imbues all security initiatives with a game-theoretic quality: Everyone sincerely hopes the entire industry will slow down, but no one wants to be the first to loosen the accelerator. Commercial competition creates a micro-level impasse, while macro-level geopolitical calculations directly lock the entire braking system in place. Amody's call to slow down, Trump's insistence on accelerating—seemingly irreconcilable, but their underlying calculations are highly overlapping: the China factor. In the White House's assessment, cutting-edge AI is a core technological asset crucial to long-term competitiveness. China's rapid progress in infrastructure construction, model iteration, and industrial applications has made Washington's decision-makers highly sensitive. From the White House's perspective, any proactive slowdown and compliance scrutiny imposed by American companies is tantamount to stopping to adjust shoelaces during the final sprint of a marathon—a unilateral strategic concession. Ammoddi's proposed slowdown strategy is similarly based on the assumption of maintaining an advantage. While suggesting a slowdown, he explicitly stated a precondition: how much the US can slow down depends on the extent of its technological lead over China. This is why, while calling for security, Amomodi still supports limiting the flow of advanced computing power and model weights. The logic is clear: the US needs time to repair its security mechanisms, provided that external pursuers are far enough away. This allows for a security buffer period to refine alignment plans. Therefore, the discussions are not purely ethical disputes; the core issue lies in balancing pace and position. Everyone hopes to reduce the risk of losing control, but in reality, no one is willing to use their relative advantages to bear this cost. It's unrealistic to expect the US AI industry to completely slam on the brakes; driven by investment from all sides and industry inertia, the technological engine will only be forced to continue roaring. A more pragmatic path in the future is to set speed limits at key junctures—routine business applications and multimodal interactions will continue to iterate rapidly, while regulatory focus will shift to clearly defined high-risk areas. Once a model is detected to have the ability to autonomously write specific high-risk code, assist in dangerous chemical experiments, or deviate from a designated safe environment, an external assessment will be forcibly triggered. Meanwhile, the post-incident reporting of major anomalies will gradually become more standardized. Regarding international communication, it is unrealistic for all parties to reach an agreement to halt research and development in the short term. Without sufficient mutual trust, a simple commitment to stop work is unlikely to truly bind all parties. A more practical approach in the future lies in establishing basic crisis communication channels. The core function of such mechanisms is to respond to sudden system anomalies. For example, when a cross-border autonomous intelligent agent experiences serious unauthorized access, or a suspected AI-induced cybersecurity incident occurs, technical personnel from all parties will have communication channels to verify the true situation and avoid misjudgments. At the very least, it needs to be agreed upon beforehand on how to ensure that two high-speed machines don't collide head-on if one party's system causes a major blunder in the physical world. From the romanticized six-month suspension letter of yesteryear to the current situation where top "car manufacturers" are forced to turn back and seek braking, technological philosophy has ultimately collided head-on with the cold reality of geopolitics. Silicon Valley's anxiety lies in the unpredictability of technological boundaries, while the White House's concern may lie in the potential loss of its hegemonic position. This posture is extremely distorted: simultaneously flooring the accelerator and frantically searching for the handbrake. However, a more crucial question remains: every player is terrified of being the first to slow down. Can those hastily cobbled-together anti-lock systems truly function in the final second before crashing into a wall?
